content:
I just discovered a feature hidden in System Settings that I never knew existed: you can set a default language for individual Mac apps. If you already knew this, there's nothing to see here, please move on. But if not, read on to find out how it works (and what doesn't)...

There are many bilingual people who switch between languages throughout the day depending on who they're talking to and what they're doing. This isn't a problem I have to deal with, but I do constantly switch between British English (and English...) and American English.

(Just to be clear, this is all in good fun! There are some usages that American English retained that British English later changed, like the -ize ending becoming -ise in British English. As James Nicoll said, "The problem with defending the purity of the English language is that English is about as pure as a cribhouse whore. It doesn't just borrow words; it sometimes goes after other languages and beats them up and steals their words too.")

Switching between the two means I can't rely on spellcheck to catch cases where I spelled the word correctly but used the wrong language version. I always assumed this was something that could only be handled manually, but today I discovered there's at least a partial solution.

At the bottom of System Preferences > General > Language & Region, there's an "Applications" section. You can add apps and select a language. Apple's American-centricity is on full display here: British English is called "English (UK)" while American English is called "English – English."

For my case, since most of my writing happens in the browser, I use two different browsers depending on the target language. My system language is set to British English, so Safari uses British English, and Chrome (listed alphabetically in the menu as Google Chrome) is set to American English.

However, as I discovered, there's an important caveat here: you can only do this for apps that support macOS's localization or language APIs, so not all apps will appear in the list.

If I am the last person on Earth to discover this feature, feel free to give me a look in the comments with your multilingual eyes.
